youtube.title: The message behind a frown | Skin Sense No. 004
youtube.caption:
Who tells your face to frown? It starts with one small, quiet message.

200 years ago, a German doctor named Justinus Kerner described a food poison found in sausages. He guessed it might one day become a medicine. So a frown is a message, and this toxin blocks it. The skin was never the target. The nerve was.

Series: Season 1: Under the surface, part 4 of 6. Next: same sun, one experiment. Which hand aged?

Sources
1. A facial muscle is told to contract by the motor nerve ending that supplies it, at the neuromuscular junction. — NIH: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34212303/
2. The motor nerve ending releases acetylcholine, the main chemical messenger (neurotransmitter) at the neuromuscular junction. — NIH: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2856357/
3. Type A's light chain is a protease that cleaves SNAP-25, a protein needed for acetylcholine vesicles to fuse with the membrane (other serotypes cut VAMP or syntaxin). — NIH: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41023315/
4. Kerner (1786–1862), a district medical officer in Württemberg, published the first accurate descriptions of food-borne botulism in 1817–1822; it followed eating meat and blood sausages. — NIH: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17458494/

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Illustrations: AI-generated, animated in code, no stock footage. Sources for every number are listed below.

Education, not medical advice. See a dermatologist about your own skin.
